subject: science
domain: Motion and Stability: Forces and Interactions
skillName: Testing a Push or Pull Design

items.prompt: What do we call the results we observe from a test?

steps: Data are the results observed from a test.

items.prompt: A ramp is meant to make a ball go faster. The ball goes faster. Did the design work?

steps: The ball did what the design intended, so it worked.

items.prompt: A wall is meant to change a ball's direction. The ball turns. Did it work?

steps: The ball changed direction as intended.

items.prompt: A ramp was meant to speed up a ball but the ball went the same speed. Did it work?

steps: The ball did not go faster, so the design did not work as intended.

items.prompt: Why do we look at data after a test?
items.answer: To see if the design worked as intended

steps: Data tell us whether the design did what we wanted.

items.prompt: If a design did not work, what can you do?
items.answer: Change the design and test again

steps: You can improve the design and test it again.

items.prompt: A pull is meant to move a toy to a basket. The toy reaches the basket. Did it work?

steps: The toy reached the basket as intended.

items.prompt: A steeper ramp makes a ball go faster than a flat ramp. Which ramp speeds it up more?

steps: The data show the steeper ramp speeds up the ball more.

items.prompt: True or false: a design works if it does what you wanted it to do.

steps: A design works when the data match the intended goal.

items.prompt: What does a ramp use to change a ball's speed?
items.answer: A push or a pull (force of the slope)

steps: The ramp uses force to speed the ball up.

items.prompt: Explain how you can tell a ramp design worked to speed up a ball.
items.answer: The data show the ball went faster than before, which was the goal

steps: If the ball went faster as intended, the design worked.

items.prompt: A design meant to turn a ball did not turn it. What should you change?
items.answer: The design, such as moving or angling the wall, then test again

steps: Changing the design and retesting can make it work.

items.prompt: Why is it helpful to compare two ramp designs with data?
items.answer: To see which one changes the ball's speed more

steps: Comparing the data shows which design works better.

items.prompt: A student wants a ball to go slower. After adding a soft surface, the ball slows. Did it work?

steps: The ball slowed as intended, so the design worked.

items.prompt: Describe how you would test if a ramp makes a ball faster.
items.answer: Roll the ball on flat ground and on the ramp and compare the speeds

steps: Comparing the speeds shows whether the ramp sped the ball up.
